analysis.title: Americas Technology: Internet - Key Takeaways from 2026 Phocuswright Conference
key_insights: AI is moving from a travel inspiration and research tool toward a transactional interface. Consumers increasingly expect AI to take actions on their behalf, but actual booking behavior is early: about 43% of travelers would book within an AI platform and only about 2% have done so (Phocuswright data).

Conference speakers disagreed on who captures the economics. Some questioned whether consumer marketplaces keep the same role once agents do comparison and shopping. Others argued AI platforms will be incremental customer acquisition channels that rely on OTAs for supply aggregation and fulfillment.

Several discussions pointed to a scenario where consumer-facing discovery shifts to AI interfaces while scaled travel platforms keep providing inventory aggregation, pricing, merchandising and servicing underneath. Speakers said newer AI entrants could underestimate the infrastructure behind the booking experience.
GS characterizes the largest potential AI risk to online travel as disintermediation of the consumer interface, not of the underlying booking infrastructure.

EXPE and BKNG continue to invest in B2B. EXPE cited its recent acquisitions (CarTrawler and Tiqets) to broaden B2B inventory and capabilities, and expects 2027 to be an important year for integrating them and speeding product deployment.
BKNG highlighted its recently announced Booking Partner Division, citing potential across airlines, financial institutions, loyalty partners and AI platforms.

Hopper highlighted growth of travel-led loyalty programs within financial services and argued payment providers and suppliers could capture more value. Hilton said about 70% of occupancy is driven by Honors customers and that it is investing in loyalty while working with AI platforms.

GS believes the conference reinforced the importance of known customers and direct relationships in an AI-driven environment, as agents gain access to loyalty accounts, payment credentials and preferences. 55% of consumers who had not connected anything to an AI agent cited privacy or security concerns.

Consumer AI usage is more pronounced for inspiration and research than for transactions. About 41% of travelers trust AI results on travel sites (about 56% of Gen Z and millennials) and about 52% use LLMs for experience planning.
GS expects 2027 to be a year of continued experimentation and integration, with transaction adoption dependent on improvements in accuracy, trust, payments and servicing.

sector_views.rationale: AI could reshape the online travel funnel, but GS sees the main risk in consumer-interface disintermediation, with OTAs likely to keep the booking infrastructure layer.

risk_factors: Disintermediation of the OTA consumer interface by AI agents and platforms.
Newer AI entrants could capture customer acquisition while OTAs bear supply and servicing complexity.
Consumer privacy and security concerns limit data sharing needed for AI personalization (55% of those not connected to an AI agent).
Slow conversion from AI interest to AI booking (about 43% willing vs about 2% done).

tension_points.bull_case: AI platforms become incremental customer acquisition channels and rely on OTAs for supply aggregation, pricing, merchandising and fulfillment, so scaled travel platforms keep the infrastructure layer.
tension_points.bear_case: Consumer marketplaces may not retain the same role if agents perform comparison and shopping, putting the OTA consumer interface at risk of disintermediation.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Transaction adoption: only about 2% of travelers have booked in an AI platform to date versus about 43% willing, so a sharp rise in AI-platform booking would challenge the OTA view.
